population_segments.name: Pregnant individuals with type 1 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: Individuals with preexisting diabetes who are planning a pregnancy or who have become pregnant should be counseled on the risk of development of diabetic embryopathy, especially anencephaly, microcephaly, congenital heart disease, kidney anomalies, and caudal regression, directly proportional to elevations in A1C during the first 10 weeks of pregnancy (13).

population_segments.name: Pregnant individuals with type 2 diabetes
population_segments.source_text: Individuals with preexisting diabetes who are planning a pregnancy or who have become pregnant should be counseled on the risk of development of diabetic embryopathy, especially anencephaly, microcephaly, congenital heart disease, kidney anomalies, and caudal regression, directly proportional to elevations in A1C during the first 10 weeks of pregnancy (13).

population_segments.name: Pregnant individuals with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
population_segments.source_text: Individuals with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) should seek preconception screening for diabetes and preconception care to identify and treat hyperglycemia and prevent congenital malformations and other adverse maternal and fetal outcomes.

synonyms: people with diabetes and childbearing potential

population_segments.source_text: Starting at puberty and continuing in all people with diabetes and childbearing potential, preconception counseling should be incorporated into routine diabetes care. A

population_segments.source_text: In pregnant individuals with diabetes and chronic hypertension, a blood pressure threshold <140/90 mmHg is recommended for initiation and titration of therapy for better pregnancy outcomes. A Therapy should be deintensified if blood pressure is <90/60 mmHg. E

specific_goals.name: A1C goal for pregnant individuals with preexisting diabetes (optimal)
specific_goals.source_text: Preconception counseling should address the importance of achieving glucose levels as close to normal as is safely possible without excessive hypoglycemia, ideally A1C <6.5% (<48 mmol/mol), to reduce the risk of congenital anomalies, preeclampsia, macrosomia, preterm birth, and other complications. A
specific_goals.rationale: to reduce the risk of congenital anomalies, preeclampsia, macrosomia, preterm birth, and other complications

specific_goals.name: A1C goal for pregnant individuals with preexisting diabetes (relaxed)
specific_goals.source_text: Ideally, the A1C goal in pregnancy is <6% (<42 mmol/mol) if this can be achieved without significant hypoglycemia, but the goal may be relaxed to <7% (<53 mmol/mol) if necessary to prevent hypoglycemia. B
specific_goals.rationale: if necessary to prevent hypoglycemia

specific_goals.name: Fasting plasma glucose goal in pregnancy
specific_goals.source_text: Glucose goals are fasting plasma glucose <95 mg/dL (<5.3 mmol/L) and either 1-h postprandial glucose <140 mg/dL (<7.8 mmol/L) or 2-h postprandial glucose <120 mg/dL (<6.7 mmol/L). B
specific_goals.rationale: to achieve optimal glucose levels

specific_goals.name: A1C goal in pregnancy (optimal)
specific_goals.source_text: In the second and third trimesters, A1C <6% (<42 mmol/mol) has the lowest risk of large-for-gestational-age infants (60,63,64), preterm delivery (65), and preeclampsia (1,66).
specific_goals.rationale: lowest risk of large-for-gestational-age infants, preterm delivery, and preeclampsia

specific_goals.name: A1C goal in pregnancy (if hypoglycemia risk)
specific_goals.source_text: Taking all of this into account, a goal of <6% (<42 mmol/mol) is optimal during pregnancy if it can be achieved without significant hypoglycemia, which, in addition to the usual adverse sequelae, may increase the risk of low birth weight (67,68).
specific_goals.rationale: if it can be achieved without significant hypoglycemia

specific_goals.name: Preprandial glucose goal in pregnancy
specific_goals.source_text: The following preconception glucose goals have been advised: preprandial glucose 80–110 mg/dL (4.4–6.1 mmol/L) and 2 h postprandial glucose <155 mg/dL (<8.6 mmol/L) (31).
specific_goals.rationale: Setting preconception glucose goals is helpful in guiding insulin dose adjustments.

specific_goals.source_text: The following preconception glucose goals have been advised: preprandial glucose 80–110 mg/dL (4.4–6.1 mmol/L) and 2 h postprandial glucose <155 mg/dL (<8.6 mmol/L) (31).
specific_goals.rationale: Setting preconception glucose goals is helpful in guiding insulin dose adjustments.

allowed_medications.name: Insulin
allowed_medications.special_instructions: None of the currently available human insulin preparations have been demonstrated to cross the placenta (102–107). Insulins studied in RCTs are preferred (108–110) over those studied in cohort studies (111), which are preferred over those studied in case reports only. Basal insulin options in pregnancy include insulin glargine (long-acting), NPH insulin (intermediate-acting), and insulin degludec (ultralong-acting). Insulin detemir (the only basal insulin with RCT data supporting its use during pregnancy) was removed from the market by the manufacturer and is no longer available. Observational studies of glargine use during pregnancy have not shown evidence of increased adverse fetal outcomes with use of insulin glargine versus NPH insulin (111), and insulin glargine is widely used during pregnancy.

allowed_medications.name: Low-dose aspirin (100-150 mg/day)
allowed_medications.special_instructions: Starting at 12–16 weeks of gestation to lower the risk of preeclampsia. A dosage of 162 mg/day may be acceptable; currently, in the U.S., low-dose aspirin is available in 81-mg tablets.

allowed_medications.name: Low-dose aspirin (81 mg/day)
allowed_medications.special_instructions: Recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force at 12 weeks of gestation in individuals at high risk for preeclampsia, such as those with type 1 or type 2 diabetes (167). However, a meta-analysis and an additional trial demonstrate that low-dose aspirin <100 mg is not effective in reducing preeclampsia, so a dose of >100 mg is required (168–170).

allowed_medications.name: Metformin (early pregnancy)
allowed_medications.special_instructions: Continuation of metformin in early pregnancy is considered safe, as first-trimester metformin use has not been associated with increased risk of major congenital malformations, and there is minimal maternal-to-fetal transfer of metformin in early gestation. When prepregnancy metformin use is continued in early pregnancy, it can be discontinued at the end of the first trimester (after organogenesis) to avoid sudden deterioration of glycemia and an associated increased risk of malformations due to hyperglycemia.

contraindicated_medications.name: Lipid-lowering medications (in most circumstances)
contraindicated_medications.reason: should be stopped prior to conception and avoided in sexually active individuals of childbearing potential with diabetes who are not using reliable contraception
contraindicated_medications.alternative: discussing the known risks and the need for more long-term safety data in offspring

contraindicated_medications.name: Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs)
contraindicated_medications.reason: should be discontinued prior to pregnancy, and contraception should be used while taking them
contraindicated_medications.alternative: initiation and titration of insulin therapy when needed to achieve preconception glycemic goals

contraindicated_medications.name: Dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and GLP-1 RAs
contraindicated_medications.reason: should be discontinued prior to pregnancy, and contraception should be used while taking them
contraindicated_medications.alternative: initiation and titration of insulin therapy when needed to achieve preconception glycemic goals

contraindicated_medications.name: Semaglutide
contraindicated_medications.reason: manufacturer prescribing information recommends discontinuation of semaglutide at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy due to its long half-life
contraindicated_medications.alternative: initiation and titration of insulin therapy when needed to achieve preconception glycemic goals

contraindicated_medications.name: Tirzepatide
contraindicated_medications.reason: Canadian manufacturer prescribing information recommends tirzepatide discontinuation at least 1 month before pregnancy
contraindicated_medications.alternative: initiation and titration of insulin therapy when needed to achieve preconception glycemic goals

contraindicated_medications.name: Metformin (in certain conditions)
contraindicated_medications.reason: due to the potential for growth restriction or acidosis in the setting of placental insufficiency, metformin should not be used in pregnant people with hypertension or preeclampsia or those at risk for intrauterine growth restriction.
contraindicated_medications.alternative: Oral agents may be an alternative for these individuals after discussing the known risks and the need for more long-term safety data in offspring.

contraindicated_medications.name: Glyburide
contraindicated_medications.reason: as both cross the placenta to the fetus and are associated with increased neonatal hypoglycemia, macrosomia, and an increased neonatal abdominal circumference.
contraindicated_medications.alternative: Insulin should be used to manage type 1 diabetes in pregnancy and is the preferred agent for the management of GDM and type 2 diabetes in pregnancy.

contraindicated_medications.name: Metformin (as first-line for GDM)
contraindicated_medications.reason: as both cross the placenta to the fetus and data on long-term safety for offspring is of some concern.
contraindicated_medications.alternative: Insulin should be used to manage type 1 diabetes in pregnancy and is the preferred agent for the management of GDM and type 2 diabetes in pregnancy.
